question: In the EU, substances of very high concern such as hexavalent chromium are subject to some of the strictest restrictions worldwide, driving European producers to innovate and invest in alternative solutions. By contrast, imports of steel products – including tinplate and electrolytic chromium coated steel manufactured with hexavalent chromium – continue to enter the EU market freely, without restriction.

This creates clear regulatory asymmetry, undermines innovation and investment in the European steel packaging sector, and weakens the EU’s strategic autonomy. The Commission has committed to proposing, by the third quarter of 2025, a measure to replace the EU’s existing steel safeguard. To be effective, a measure of this nature needs to also achieve reciprocity in global sustainability standards: 1.

When and how will the Commission propose to address the restriction on imports of products/articles manufactured using substances that are banned for use in processes within the EU but that can be freely used outside of the EU with the resulting products imported without restriction into the EU – such as steel products produced with hexavalent chromium?

How will the post-safeguard regime be designed to ensure reciprocity in standards and reinforce the Steel Action Plan’s capacity objectives, and will it include a stricter tariffrate quota system – for example, through reduced volumes and higher above-quota tariffs?
Will the new measure take effect by the first quarter of 2026?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.12.

2025) The use of hexavalent chromium substances is subject to several complementary pieces of EU legislation, for example, Regulation (EC) No 1907/20061 concerning the Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH), and Directive 2004/37/EC2 on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens, mutagens or reprotoxic substances at work (CMRD).

The Commission has no concrete plans for import restrictions on hexavalent chromiumtreated steel products but is preparing to shift hexavalent chromium substances from authorisation to restriction under REACH. The current phase of this transition process is the development of opinions by the scientific committees of the European Chemicals Agency.

The Commission is studying the health and economic impact of a possible revision of the occupational exposure limit for chromium VI compounds under CMRD. Such revision would contribute to workers’ protection, while avoiding excessive burden. The current work is informed by scientific evidence, such as a Risk Assessment Committee of European Chemical Agency Opinion, and subject to stakeholder input.

The scope of the planned steel measure proposed on 7 October 20253 does not include reciprocity in standards. Its core policy objective is to address the trade-related negative effects of global overcapacity by limiting imports into the EU’s market. Potential actions on standards may need to be addressed through other policy initiatives.
Its enforcement date depends on co-legislators, with the current steel safeguards set to expire at the end of June 2026.
